Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3

src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
 Mandatory 13
File
oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:17-45
oracle-init/create-user.sh:19-37

Explanation

The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single deployable application with server-rendered gallery pages and a JSON upload response. Diagrams describe the inspected implementation, not the Azure migration proposed by the workshop README.

Data Storage & External Services

Uploads store bytes in the database alongside metadata; the image-serving controller constructs an in-memory resource from those bytes. The Compose oracle_data volume persists Oracle database files, not a directory of uploaded images. A checked-in static upload image and a test upload-path property are legacy artifacts, not evidence of the current upload destination. No cache, broker, or backend cloud API integration is present in the inspected source. The browser separately requests Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr.

Evidence: /home/runner/work/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite/src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:36-41; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:116-166; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:57-83; docker-compose.yml:3-16; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7,124. Here and below, relative evidence paths resolve against /home/runner/work/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite/.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Constructor injection connects controllers to a service interface and its implementation to a repository.
  • Database-backed binary storage is authoritative; there is no filesystem write or file-resource serving path in the photo service/controller.
  • The application uses transaction-scoped services and Oracle-specific repository SQL rather than inter-service calls.

DTOs & Contracts

  • MultipartFile is the framework request contract. No dedicated upload request DTO exists.
  • Mutable UploadResult is an internal per-file service outcome, transformed by HomeController into JSON maps rather than returned directly.
  • Mutable domain entity Photo is supplied to HTML views and used to compose successful upload metadata; it is not returned as the entire entity in the JSON upload response. See data-architecture.md for its fields and persistence.
  • The upload JSON envelope contains a Boolean success indicator plus successful metadata entries and file-name/error entries. A nonempty batch can return HTTP 200 with success=false if every file fails; mixed outcomes are supported.
  • There are no gateway aggregation DTOs, immutable records, custom serialization configuration, OpenAPI, protobuf, or GraphQL contracts in the inspected application files. JSON uses the Boot web/JSON stack; no custom date representation is specified locally.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-47; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-155; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:58-97; pom.xml:32-40,75-79.

Communication Patterns

Browser requests synchronously invoke controllers, PhotoService and the repository. The browser's asynchronous JavaScript fetch does not establish broker-based asynchronous service communication. No outbound backend HTTP/gRPC client, message broker, event choreography, discovery registry, gateway aggregation, client-side balancing, retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead or application timeout is defined in the inspected source. Consequently there are no configured retry counts, service timeout values or circuit-breaker fallbacks to report.

The gallery deliberately degrades to an empty view after a read failure; detail failures redirect, image failures return 500, and upload errors are represented per file. These are local error paths, not resilience-library fallback policies. Compose starts the app after the database health condition; see configuration-inventory.md for startup details.

Security is present: the two write routes require authentication through stateless HTTP Basic and an in-memory BCrypt-encoded admin identity. Reads are public; the ADMIN role is assigned but no role-specific or per-photo ownership check is applied. CSRF is explicitly disabled. No JWT/OAuth, application TLS or HTTPS connector is configured; Compose publishes HTTP, so external transport protection cannot be assumed. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-59; docker-compose.yml:32-43.

Service Communication Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Client as "Browser" participant Security as "Security filter chain" participant Controller as "HomeController" participant Service as "PhotoService" participant Repo as "PhotoRepository" participant DB as "Oracle" Client->>Security: POST /upload with multipart files and Basic credentials alt Authentication fails Security-->>Client: 401 authentication challenge else Authenticated Security->>Controller: Forward multipart request loop Each supplied file Controller->>Service: uploadPhoto MultipartFile alt Validation or read fails Service-->>Controller: UploadResult failure else Accepted Service->>Repo: Save Photo including bytes Repo->>DB: Persist record DB-->>Repo: Saved record or database error Repo-->>Service: Photo or exception Service-->>Controller: UploadResult success or failure opt Successful upload Controller->>Service: Retrieve Photo for response metadata Service->>Repo: findById Repo-->>Service: Optional Photo Service-->>Controller: Photo metadata end end end Controller-->>Client: 200 JSON success and per-file outcomes end

The no-files/handled-multipart-error branch returns 400 before the loop; no retry is applied. Transaction-completion failures or the post-save metadata lookup can escape the local result-construction path, so the per-file failure envelope is not guaranteed for every infrastructure exception.

Evidence: Dockerfile:24-31; docker-compose.yml:11-24,32-53.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose first validates required ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD substitutions.
  2. Oracle container starts and runs mounted schema scripts using supplied credentials. One script includes a fixed 30-second sleep; both check whether the schema user exists (oracle-init/create-user.sh:15-39; oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:22-43).
  3. Database health is checked with SQL SELECT 1 FROM DUAL via SQLPlus using the application schema account: 30-second interval, 10-second timeout, 15 retries, 180-second start period (docker-compose.yml:19-24). These are configured checks, not proof of actual readiness.
  4. App waits on Compose service_healthy for Oracle, then starts with docker profile (docker-compose.yml:41-46). Outside Compose no explicit wait mechanism is configured; database/admin properties must be available at context creation.

No config-server/discovery chain, dockerize wrapper, application startup retry policy, Kubernetes readiness dependency or separately configured app startup timeout is present. Management route inventory belongs in api-service-contracts.md.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Operator supplies values through the local environment or copies .env.example to ignored .env and replaces placeholders; Compose passes the database admin/schema credentials into Oracle and binds the schema password into the application datasource environment. Initialization connects as SYSTEM to create/check the schema user and applies schema-scoped grants; the app then connects as that user. Admin credentials feed the application's in-memory user service. No managed identity, service principal, cloud secret-store role, encryption wrapper, sealed secret or CI secret-fetch workflow is implemented in these files.

Core Business Workflows

Users browse a shared photo gallery, inspect photos and navigate chronologically. Authenticated operators upload one or more images and remove photos, receiving per-file or page-level feedback.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
Photo Album deployable / PhotoServiceImplGallery management, upload and removalPhoto; transient UploadResultDatabase repository; local image-header inspection

There are no independent domain microservices. All three controllers use the same photo service; the shared application is the source of truth rather than a gateway combining remote owners.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch of photos

  1. User selects/drops files; browser applies the client upload filter, submits the accepted subset and displays progress.
  2. The write request must pass authenticated-write access. HomeController applies batch presence validation, then calls the service separately for each file.
  3. Service applies server upload validation, reads bytes, applies image-header safety validation when a reader exists, and creates the photo.
  4. The photo including binary content is saved to the database. No durable filesystem upload step occurs.
  5. For successful service outcomes, the controller looks up the saved photo and composes response metadata. It combines successes and failures, permitting partial success, then the browser prepends successful cards and displays errors.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-132,135-159; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:51-58.

Workflow 2: Browse, inspect and navigate

  1. Gallery requests all photos newest first; a read error produces an empty gallery rather than an error page.
  2. Selecting a photo loads its record and computes older/newer neighbors by timestamp. Missing IDs, absent records or read errors redirect to the gallery.
  3. The browser separately retrieves image bytes from the database-backed image controller. A missing record or missing binary content yields not found; other serving failures yield an internal error.
  4. Available adjacent IDs become navigation links. There is no wraparound when no older/newer photo is found.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:38-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:215-229.

Workflow 3: Remove a photo

  1. Browser displays a confirmation prompt before submitting the deletion.
  2. After write authentication, the service looks up the photo; missing records produce a not-found outcome.
  3. Existing photo rows, including their stored image bytes, are deleted. The controller redirects to the gallery with success/not-found/error feedback.

There is no soft-delete state, restore workflow, remote cleanup or filesystem unlink operation. Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-51; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-208.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service orchestration, gateway aggregation, message exchange or asynchronous business processing exists in the inspected implementation. HomeController's upload metadata lookup and DetailController's adjacent-photo composition are in-process combinations over one service/repository. There is no downstream service outage fallback or circuit breaker; the empty-gallery, redirect, per-file error and image-error behaviors are local handling paths.

The database container is infrastructure, not a second domain service. Browser CDN requests supply styling/scripts rather than business data.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Gallery operator" participant Browser as "Upload interface" participant Access as "Write access check" participant Controller as "Upload controller" participant Service as "Photo service" participant Photo as "New Photo" participant Store as "Photo database" User->>Browser: Select or drop images Browser->>Browser: Apply client upload filter Browser->>Access: Submit accepted files alt Credentials missing or invalid Access-->>Browser: Authentication challenge Browser-->>User: Upload failure feedback else Authenticated Access->>Controller: Accept upload request loop Each file in batch Controller->>Service: Attempt upload Service->>Service: Check server upload and image-header rules alt Rejected or unreadable file Service-->>Controller: File-specific failure else Accepted image Service->>Photo: Create image and metadata record Service->>Store: Save photo including binary bytes alt Persistence succeeds Store-->>Service: Saved photo Service-->>Controller: Successful photo identifier Controller->>Service: Obtain saved display metadata Service-->>Controller: Photo metadata else Save operation reports error Store-->>Service: Persistence exception Service-->>Controller: File-specific save failure end end end Controller-->>Browser: Combined successes and failures Browser-->>User: New gallery cards and per-file feedback end

The save-error branch describes the local catch path, not a guarantee that every transaction-completion error is converted into an upload result. No automated retry or compensating rollback across the entire batch is implemented.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

RuleActual implementation and limitsEvidence
Client upload filterAllows JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP MIME labels; rejects files over 10 MiB. This is UI guidance, not authoritative server validation.upload.js:65-79
Batch presence validationEmpty/null file list and handled multipart failures return a bad request; nonempty batches are processed file by file.HomeController.java:63-70,100-106
Server upload validationLowercased declared content type must be allowed; byte size must be positive and not exceed configured maximum. Missing MIME may enter the generic failure path.PhotoServiceImpl.java:85-109,178-181
Image-header safety validationReader-provided width × height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels. Reads header dimensions rather than fully decoding. IOException rejects upload; other extraction exceptions permit continuing without dimensions. No matching reader also permits continuing, so this is not full image-content validation.PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-34,116-152
Metadata constraintsFilename is nonblank and at most 255 characters; size nonnull and positive; MIME nonblank and at most 50 characters; upload time nonnull. No request-level Valid annotation is used; entity constraints are declared for persistence validation.Photo.java:31-64; HomeController.java:58
Declared batch-count settingConfiguration says 10 files per upload, but controller loops all supplied files and service does not consume/enforce this value. Multipart request-size limit is separate.application.properties:24-30; HomeController.java:69-91; PhotoServiceImpl.java:40-46
Partial successResponse success means at least one saved photo was successfully reread and added to response metadata. All-file failures still produce a normal JSON response for a nonempty processed batch. No batch-wide atomicity is defined.HomeController.java:69-97
Chronological neighborsStrictly earlier/later timestamps; previous candidates descending, next ascending and not later than database current time; service selects first candidate. Equal-time photos are not neighbors through these predicates.PhotoRepository.java:37-62; PhotoServiceImpl.java:215-229
Photo identity/lifecycleConstruction assigns UUID and current local timestamp; lifecycle is create, read and hard delete, with no workflow status or state machine.Photo.java:79-90; PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-205
Authenticated-write accessUpload/delete require authentication; reads are public. Assigned ADMIN role is not checked explicitly; no per-photo owner access rule. HTTP Basic is stateless, CSRF disabled, no local TLS configuration.SecurityConfig.java:33-58

In this table, Java short filenames refer to src/main/java/com/photoalbum/ under their corresponding controller/model/repository/service/config packages; upload.js is under src/main/resources/static/js/ and application.properties under src/main/resources/.

Transactions and integrity: service class is transactional; reads are marked read-only. Each controller-issued service upload is a separate operation; binary content and metadata share the entity write. No bidirectional associations or cross-service saga/compensation are needed by the current model. Caught persistence exceptions may still mark a transaction rollback-only or surface at commit.

Errors and audit: service reads/deletes wrap failures in runtime exceptions; upload generally produces UploadResult errors, and controllers apply their local feedback policies. There are SLF4J upload/delete/error logs, but no dedicated immutable audit trail, entity change history or dead-letter queue. Image serving logs filenames and initial bytes. Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

One JPA entity stores photo metadata and binary content in Oracle; the test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database. There are no entity-to-entity relationships.

Entity Model

erDiagram %% All entities belong to photo-album Photo { string id PK "UUID string, length 36" string original_file_name "Required, length 255" bytes photo_data "Nullable database LOB" long file_size "Required" string mime_type "Required, length 50" datetime uploaded_at "Required, indexed" int width "Nullable" int height "Nullable" }

Photo maps to photos; idx_photos_uploaded_at is a nonunique index. Java types are String, byte array, Long, String, LocalDateTime and nullable Integer dimensions. The constructor generates a UUID and local timestamp. The binary column is explicitly nullable even though normal accepted uploads supply bytes. There are no foreign keys, cascade rules, bidirectional associations, or explicit lazy BLOB mapping. Full entity queries select photo_data, including the unpaginated gallery query; metadata-only projection is not implemented.

PhotoServiceImpl has a class-level transaction boundary, with read-only annotations for gallery, lookup and navigation operations. Upload and delete use write transactions. Catching a repository failure while constructing an upload result does not guarantee the transaction can subsequently commit.

Caching Strategy

No Spring Cache annotations, cache provider dependency, explicit TTL/eviction policy, JCache binding, Redis service, query cache or Hibernate second-level cache configuration was found in the inspected application and configuration. JPA's normal persistence context is not evidence of a shared application cache.

Image responses explicitly prohibit browser/proxy caching; the upload script additionally appends a timestamp to image URLs. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:74-83; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179; pom.xml:30-101.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The single application owns one database schema for reads and writes. Controllers share the same in-process service/repository rather than separate service-owned stores. There is no cross-service database access, event replication, gateway aggregation, outbox or CQRS read model. Test H2 is a separate testing context, not a second production data owner.
